title: String methods and f-strings
subtitle: Clean messy text and format output like a pro
goal: Clean and analyse text with string methods, and produce polished, aligned output with f-strings.
outcomes: Call string methods like strip, lower, replace and split, and chain them
Search text with find, count, startswith and endswith
Check whether text is all digits with isdigit
Build output with f-strings, including expressions inside the braces
Format money and columns with :.2f, :, and alignment specs

slides.title: Mission 5: Clean text, beautiful output
slides.body:
Real text is messy: `"  RIYA@Gmail.COM "` from a sign-up form, a city typed five different ways.

Today you'll **clean** text with string methods and **format** polished output with f-strings, all the way to a printed receipt.
slides.say: Welcome to day five. Text from real users is messy: extra spaces, random capitals, inconsistent spellings. Today you'll learn the string methods developers use to clean it up, and f strings, the modern way to produce polished output like receipts, tables and reports.

slides.title: Methods: functions that belong to a value
slides.body:
A **method** is called with a dot: `city.upper()`.

Strings are immutable (Day 4), so a method never changes the original. It **returns a new string** that you print or store.
slides.say: A method is a function that belongs to a value. You call it with a dot after the value, like city dot upper. Remember from yesterday that strings are immutable. So a string method never changes the original. It hands you back a brand new string, and if you want to keep it, you assign it to a name.

slides.title: Case and whitespace
slides.code:
city = "  new DELHI  "
print(city.upper())
print(city.lower())
print(city.title())
print(city.strip())
print(city.strip().title())   # chain: left to right
print(len(city), len(city.strip()))
print(city)                   # unchanged!
slides.expect:
NEW DELHI  
  new delhi  
  New Delhi  
new DELHI
New Delhi
13 9
  new DELHI
explain: Capital first letter for each word.
Chaining: strip() returns a string, then .title() runs on it.
Methods return new strings; city is untouched.
slides.say: Upper, lower and title change the case. Strip removes spaces from both ends, which is the first thing you should do with any text a user types. Line six chains two methods: strip runs first, then title runs on its result. The length line proves the spaces are gone, and the last line proves the original string never changed.

slides.title: Search and replace
slides.code:
review = "The food was good. The service was good too."
print(review.replace("good", "great"))
print(review.count("good"))
print(review.find("service"))
print(review.find("price"))       # -1 means not found
print(review.startswith("The"))
print(review.endswith("!"))
slides.expect:
The food was great. The service was great too.
2
23
-1
True
False
explain: True or False: does it start with 'The'?
slides.say: Replace swaps every match for new text. Count tells you how many times something appears. Find returns the index where a match starts, or minus one if it isn't there, so always watch for that minus one. Startswith and endswith answer yes or no questions with True or False, a type you'll use to make decisions on day seven.

slides.title: split and join
slides.body:
- `text.split(",")` cuts text into a **list** of pieces
- `text.split()` splits on any run of spaces
- `" | ".join(pieces)` glues pieces with a separator

You'll master lists on Day 11. For now: a list is a row of numbered slots, indexed like a string.
slides.say: Split cuts a string into pieces wherever it finds a separator, and gives you a list of the pieces. With no argument, it splits on spaces, tabs and new lines. Join does the reverse: it glues pieces together with the separator you call it on. You'll master lists on day eleven. For now, a list is a row of numbered slots, indexed just like a string.

slides.title: Parse a CSV line
slides.code:
row = "Riya Sharma,21,Pune,riya@example.com"
parts = row.split(",")
print(parts)
print(parts[0])
print(parts[-1])

tags = "python   ai  web"
words = tags.split()
print(words)
print(" | ".join(words))
print("-".join("2026 10 18".split()))
slides.expect:
['Riya Sharma', '21', 'Pune', 'riya@example.com']
Riya Sharma
riya@example.com
['python', 'ai', 'web']
python | ai | web
2026-10-18
explain: Cut at every comma: a list of 4 strings.
No argument: split on any run of spaces.
Glue the words back together with ' | '.
Split, then join: spaces become dashes.
slides.say: A line from a CSV file holds several fields separated by commas. Split turns it into a list, and indexes pull out each field: index zero is the name and minus one is the email. Split with no argument copes with messy spacing between words. Join then rebuilds the text with any separator you like.

slides.title: Clean an email
slides.code:
email = "  Riya.S@Gmail.com "
clean = email.strip().lower()
print(clean)
print(clean.split("@")[1])
slides.why: strip() removes the outer spaces and lower() fixes the case. split("@") gives ['riya.s', 'gmail.com'], and index 1 is the domain.
slides.say: Predict both lines. First we clean the email, then we split it at the at sign and take the piece at index one. What do you get?

slides.title: isdigit: is it a number?
slides.code:
pin = "411001"
print(pin.isdigit())
print("4110O1".isdigit())     # a letter O, not a zero
print("".isdigit())
print("-5".isdigit())
print("12.5".isdigit())
print(" 42 ".strip().isdigit())
slides.expect:
True
False
False
False
False
True
explain: All six characters are digits: True.
One character is the letter O: False.
Empty text has no digits: False.
The minus sign isn't a digit.
slides.say: Isdigit returns True only when every character is a digit and the string isn't empty. It's the quickest check before turning user input into a number. Notice the traps: a letter O hiding among zeros, an empty string, a minus sign and a decimal point all give False. Stripping spaces first makes the check fair.

slides.title: The forgotten result
slides.why: upper() returns a new string, but this code throws it away. name still points to the original 'riya'. To keep the result, write name = name.upper().
slides.say: A trap that bites every beginner. We call upper on name, then print name. What appears?

slides.title: Fix the sign-up form
slides.task: This form should save a clean username: no spaces around it, all lowercase. It prints `[  Riya_Codes  ]` instead of `[riya_codes]`. Fix it.
slides.starter:
username = "  Riya_Codes  "
username.strip()
username.lower()
print("Saved username: [" + username + "]")
slides.solution:
username = "  Riya_Codes  "
username = username.strip().lower()
print("Saved username: [" + username + "]")
slides.tests:
assert username == "riya_codes", f"username is still {username!r}. strip() and lower() return NEW strings: store the result, for example username = username.strip()."
assert "[riya_codes]" in __out__, "Print the cleaned username inside the brackets."
hints: Strings are immutable. A method gives back a new string; it doesn't change the old one.
Assign the result back: username = username.strip().lower()
slides.say: This sign up form should save a clean, lowercase username without spaces. But the saved value is still messy. Work out why, and fix it. Hint: think about what a method does, and doesn't do, to the original string.

slides.title: f-strings: the modern way to format
slides.body:
Put `f` before the quotes and drop values straight into `{ }`:
`f"Hi {name}, you have {count} messages"`

Any expression works inside the braces: `{qty * price}`, `{name.upper()}`. Numbers just work, no conversion needed.

visual.verdict: One readable string, values exactly where you want them.

slides.say: F strings are the modern way to build text. Put the letter f just before the opening quote, then write any variable or expression inside curly braces, right where you want it in the sentence. Python fills in the value. No plus signs, no fiddling with spaces, and numbers just work. Professional Python code uses f strings everywhere.

slides.title: f-strings with expressions
slides.code:
name = "Kabir"
item = "Masala chai"
qty = 3
price = 25

print(f"Hi {name}!")
print(f"{qty} x {item} = {qty * price} rupees")
print(f"Shouting: {name.upper()}")
print(f"{name} has {len(name)} letters")
print(f"{qty=}, {price=}")    # a debugging trick
slides.expect:
Hi Kabir!
3 x Masala chai = 75 rupees
Shouting: KABIR
Kabir has 5 letters
qty=3, price=25
explain: {qty=} prints the name and the value: great for debugging.
slides.say: Inside the braces you can put any expression: a calculation, a method call, even len. Python works it out and drops the result into the text. The last line is a favourite debugging trick. Put an equals sign after a name inside the braces, and Python prints both the name and its value.

slides.title: Format specs
slides.body: After a **colon** inside the braces, a format spec controls how the value looks.
slides.say: Add a colon inside the braces and you get format specs, a tiny language for presentation. Point two f shows exactly two decimal places, perfect for money. A comma adds thousands separators. And the arrow and caret symbols align text inside a fixed width: right, left or centre. That's how you build neat tables in a terminal.

slides.title: Money and alignment
slides.code:
total = 1234.5
gst = total * 0.18
print(f"Total: {total:.2f}")
print(f"GST:   {gst:.2f}")
print(f"Salary: {1250000:,} rupees")
print(f"Grand total: ₹{total + gst:,.2f}")

print(f"[{'chai':<10}]")
print(f"[{'chai':>10}]")
print(f"[{'chai':^10}]")
print(f"[{42:>6}]")
slides.expect:
Total: 1234.50
GST:   222.21
Salary: 1,250,000 rupees
Grand total: ₹1,456.71
[chai      ]
[      chai]
[   chai   ]
[    42]
explain: Pad to 10 characters, text on the left.
slides.say: Point two f always shows two decimals, so one thousand two hundred thirty four point five is shown as point five zero, the way money should look. The GST is rounded for display too. Comma adds separators to big numbers. In the second half, the square brackets make the padding visible: left, right and centre inside ten characters.

slides.title: A formatted receipt
slides.body: Widths add up to 32 characters per line, so every column lines up.
slides.code:
shop = "Monsoon Cafe, Pune"
item1, qty1, price1 = "Masala chai", 12, 25
item2, qty2, price2 = "Veg sandwich", 8, 80
item3, qty3, price3 = "Brownie", 6, 65

total1 = qty1 * price1
total2 = qty2 * price2
total3 = qty3 * price3
subtotal = total1 + total2 + total3
gst = subtotal * 0.05
grand = subtotal + gst

print(f"{shop:^32}")
print("-" * 32)
print(f"{item1:<16}{qty1:>4}{total1:>12,.2f}")
print(f"{item2:<16}{qty2:>4}{total2:>12,.2f}")
print(f"{item3:<16}{qty3:>4}{total3:>12,.2f}")
print("-" * 32)
print(f"{'Subtotal':<20}{subtotal:>12,.2f}")
print(f"{'GST 5%':<20}{gst:>12,.2f}")
print(f"{'TOTAL (₹)':<20}{grand:>12,.2f}")
explain: Multiple assignment from Day 2: three values in one line.
Centre the shop name in 32 characters.
16 for the name, 4 for the quantity, 12 for the amount.
Text can be aligned with a spec too.
slides.say: Here's everything together: a real receipt. Each line uses widths and alignment, so item names line up on the left and amounts line up on the right, with exactly two decimals. Big totals get a thousands separator. Change a quantity and run it again. The layout stays perfect. This is how billing systems print a bill.

slides.title: Pick the format
slides.why: :, adds separators and .2f gives two decimals. Combine them as :,.2f. The first option prints 1499.00 and the second prints 1,499.
slides.say: Quick check. The price is fourteen ninety nine. Which f string displays it with a thousands separator and two decimal places?

slides.title: Normalise a phone number
slides.task:
Users type phone numbers every way imaginable. Turn `raw` into `phone`: just the 10 digits.
- strip the spaces around it
- remove `+91`, dashes and inner spaces with `replace()`

Print `phone` and `phone.isdigit()`.
slides.tests:
import re
def again(r):
    ns = {}
    exec(re.sub(r"^raw\s*=.*$", f'raw = "{r}"', __code__, count=1, flags=re.M), ns)
    return ns["phone"]
assert "phone" in globals(), "Create a variable called phone."
assert phone == "9876543210", f"phone should be '9876543210', but it is {phone!r}. Remove +91, dashes and spaces."
assert again("98765 43210") == "9876543210", "For '98765 43210' you should get '9876543210'. Remove the space in the middle too."
assert again("+91-91234-56789") == "9123456789", "For '+91-91234-56789' you should get '9123456789'."
assert again("  080-2345 6789 ") == "08023456789", "A landline like '  080-2345 6789 ' should become '08023456789'. Chain your replace() calls on raw."
assert "True" in __out__, "Also print phone.isdigit(), so you can see the result is digits only."
hints: replace("-", "") deletes every dash; replace(" ", "") deletes every space.
slides.say: Users type phone numbers every way imaginable: with the country code, with dashes, with spaces. Write one line of chained methods that turns any of them into plain digits. Then print isdigit to prove it worked.

slides.title: Payment confirmation
slides.task:
Build `message` with an f-string, like a payments app:
`Paid ₹2,500.00 to Ravi Kumar`

- the payee's name stripped and in title case
- the amount with separators and 2 decimals

Print `message`.
slides.starter:
payee = "  ravi kumar "
amount = 2500
# message = f"..."
slides.solution:
payee = "  ravi kumar "
amount = 2500
message = f"Paid ₹{amount:,.2f} to {payee.strip().title()}"
print(message)
slides.tests:
import re
def again(p, a):
    src = re.sub(r"^payee\s*=.*$", f'payee = "{p}"', __code__, count=1, flags=re.M)
    src = re.sub(r"^amount\s*=.*$", f"amount = {a}", src, count=1, flags=re.M)
    ns = {}
    exec(src, ns)
    return ns["message"]
assert "message" in globals(), "Create a variable called message."
assert message == "Paid ₹2,500.00 to Ravi Kumar", f"message should be 'Paid ₹2,500.00 to Ravi Kumar', but it is {message!r}."
assert again("ANITA", 99.5) == "Paid ₹99.50 to Anita", "For payee 'ANITA' and amount 99.5 you should get 'Paid ₹99.50 to Anita'. Use :,.2f and .title()."
assert again(" dev ", 1234567.891) == "Paid ₹1,234,567.89 to Dev", "For 1234567.891 the amount should show as ₹1,234,567.89."
assert message in __out__, "Print the message."
hints: Clean the name inside the braces too: {payee.strip().title()}
slides.say: Every payments app shows a confirmation like paid two thousand five hundred rupees to Ravi Kumar. Build that message with a single f string. Clean the payee's name, and format the amount with separators and two decimals.

slides.title: Mission 5 complete
points: Methods return new strings: strip, lower, upper, title, replace; chain them left to right
find, count, startswith and endswith search text; find returns -1 when nothing matches
split() cuts text into a list; join() glues pieces with a separator
isdigit() checks for digits only before you convert
f"{value:,.2f}" and :<, :>, :^ give money and columns a professional look
slides.say: Mission five complete. You can clean messy text, search it, split it into fields, and format beautiful output with f strings. Tomorrow your programs start listening: you'll read input from the user and convert it into numbers. See you on day six.
